# Chemical characterisation of spent rechargeable batteries

Ivano Vassura, Luciano Morselli, Elena Bernardi, Fabrizio Passarini \*

a r t i c l e i n f o

Article history: Accepted 30 March 2009 Available online 6 May 2009

## ABSTRACT

A chemical characterisation of used batteries can give useful information to implement suitable recycling techniques and to estimate the flux of the different materials recovered. This work is aimed to provide quantitative data about the composition of mixed batteries (in particular, Ni–Cd, Ni-MH and Li-ion batteries) collected in a Northern Italian town in order to evaluate the feasibility of recovery processes applied to the selected material. The higher concentration of metals in the <3 mm fraction suggested that significant quantities of valuable elements could be recovered: in particular, for a kg of the <3 mm fraction deriving from disassembled batteries, about 390 g Ni and 330 g Cd can be recovered from Ni–Cd, 630 g Ni, 80 g Co from Ni-MH and 250 g Co, 110 g Ni, 120 g Cu from Li-ion ones. Leaching tests applied to the same fractions, to assess possible contaminant releases, resulted in low metal content in aqueous solutions (except for Al and Fe, the concentrations of all metals remained below 1 mg/kg). Even so, great care is required in all handling activities due to the high pH values of leachate solutions.

\- 2009 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.

## 1. Introduction

Each year, more than 13,000 tons of rechargeable portable batteries are sold in Europe (EPBA, 2006). Recycling is an important issue not only from a waste treatment perspective, but also for the recovery of valuable materials, as nickel and cobalt metals and some of their salts (Rabah et al., 2008), together with copper and rare earth (Nan et al., 2006), or also cadmium and zinc (Pietrelli et al., 2005) and lithium (Paulino et al., 2008).

A research project concerning the management of spent rechargeable batteries (RB) was implemented by TRED Carpi s.r.l. (Modena, Northern Italy), as part of a LIFE project (named P.I.R.R.) in order to foster portable battery management and recycling in Italy. To support this project, an analytical characterisation of the rechargeable batteries collected and pre-treated by the industrial company was performed in laboratory.

A battery is composed of an external case (made of steel, polymeric materials or paperboard), separators (made of polymeric materials, paper or paperboard), electrical joints (metals as Cu), electrodes, and electrolytes. Simple separation processes can recover some homogeneous material fractions as ABS polymer, or metallic scraps. Recovery of metals such as Ni, Cd, or Li, found in the electrolytic cell (electrodes and electrolytes), can be subject to different recycling processes, including the mineral processing techniques of pyrometallurgical or hydrometallurgical treatment (Bernardes et al., 2004).

However, in order to promote the recycling of this kind of batteries, it is necessary to know their composition. According to the producers’ estimates (EPBA, 2007), indicative chemical compositions of these kinds of battery (as a whole) are:

– Ni–Cd: Fe (40%), Ni (22%), Cd (15%), plastic (5%), KOH (2%), others (16%).

– Ni-MH: Ni (33%), Fe (30%), lanthanides (10%), H O (8%), Co (3%), plastic (5%), KOH (2%), Mn (1%), Zn (1%), others (7%).

– Li-ion: Al (15–25%), carbon amorphous powder (0.1–1%), Cu foil (5–15%), diethyl carbonate (DEC) (1–10%), ethylene carbonate (EC) (1–10%), methyl ethyl carbonate (MEC) (1–10%), LiPF (1– 5%), graphite powder (10–30%), LiCoO (25–45%), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) (0.5–2%), steel, Ni and inert polymer.

The aim of the present work is to determine the actual average composition of the main types of spent rechargeable batteries coming from the collection and pre-treatment system operating in Modena city. Leaching tests on the samples were also performed to estimate possible environmental releases (USEPA, 1999; Karnchanawong and Limpiteeprakan, 2009), which could occur particularly in the critical steps of storage, transport and possible recycling of the material.

## 2. Experimental

The entire procedure followed in the present study is reported in Fig. 1. The collection ofabout 200 kg ofspent rechargeable batteries, varying for technology, use and brand, was performed in 3 months by placing several different selective boxes nearby electric and elec tronic stores in Modena Province. The following manual separation sorted three most important kinds of batteries: Ni–Cd (40.1% in weight), Ni-MH (34.5%) and Li–ion (7.5%). The remaining 18% were batteries with abraded and illegible labels, uncommon ones (e.g., Lipolymers/Li-hydrogen) or incorrectly disposed ones (e.g. single use batteries), which were not included in the study.

Each selected battery type was fed into a continuous milling machine for size reduction, and a fractionation process was then applied, separating the materials in a coarse fraction >3 mm (including the plastic of external shell, residual plastic pieces and felt and cardboard from internal battery protection), and a fine fraction <3 mm (mainly made up of metallic powder deriving from electrodes).

This process was not made to provide a high quality separation of specific materials, but in order to obtain an economic, rough separation of metal-rich fractions. About 1 kg of the <3 mm fraction for each kind of battery was used for chemical characterisation tests.

## 2.1. Sample preparation

In the laboratory, after a magnetic separation of the coarse ferrous residues contained in Ni–Cd batteries, all samples were divided through a suitable sieve into two further size fractions: U < 1 mm and 1 mm < U < 3 mm. In this way, a possible difference in metal concentration in the various fractions was investigated.

At the end, from the three original samples, seven fractions were obtained as reported in Fig. 1.

## 2.2. Weight loss determination (105 C)

Weight loss, mainly due to the vaporisation of moisture and other volatile compounds, was determined by drying the samples to a constant mass at 105 C (about 3–4 h were needed). All data reported refer to dry weight.

## 2.3. Chemical characterisation

About 5 mg of each sample fraction were digested with 8 ml of HNO /HCl Suprapur (ratio 1/3) in a closed Teflon vessel, at 210 C, for 15 min in a microwave oven. Then, the solutions were diluted with deionised water as needed.

All metals except mercury were measured by ICP/AES; mercury was analysed by cold vapour atomic absorption spectrometry (CVAAS).

## 2.4. Leaching test

Leaching tests were performed according to European Standard Procedures (EN – 12457 – 2). All the seven sub-samples (reported in Fig. 1) were put in contact with distilled water in capped bottles. Liquid to solid ratio was 10/1 and the suspension was agitated by an overhead shaker (5 rpm) for 24 h at room temperature (20 ± 5 ^).. Solid residue was separated by filtration. In eluates, pH, F-, Cl-, SO2-, NO- were analysed by ionic chromatography (IC). After acidification (pH = 2 using HNO ) metals were measured using the same methods followed for digested samples.

## 3. Results and discussion

Limits of quantification and the mean coefficients of variance registered for each metal (in%) in the digested and leachate solutions were found from three different sub-samples of each classification, and are reported in Table 1. It can be observed that the heterogeneous nature of materials led to some significant CV% for some metals. The lower precision for Al and Mn can be ascribed to the low concentrations registered in solutions, while for Fe it can be attributed to its presence in coarser particles, which renders the sampling of a representative aliquot for the analysis rather more difficult. However, other heavy metals resulted in a CV% on average in the range 10–20%, which can be considered good analytic precision. Chemical composition (wt%) of the seven battery sub-samples are reported in Table 2.

## 3.1. Ni–Cd batteries

## 3.1.1. Weight loss

The weight loss of Ni–Cd battery samples was 6.55% for the finer fraction (size <1 mm), 6.19% for the fraction 1 mm < U < 3 mm and 2.68% for the ferrous fraction, which could be ascribed to a partial loss of electrolyte solution (water from potassium hydroxide solution). However, the not negligible weight loss unexpectedly measured even in the ferrous fraction was probably due to the moisture of the dust adhered to the surface of the metal fragments manually selected by means of a magnet.

## 3.1.2. Metal content

The finer fraction (size <1 mm) consists of 41% in weight both of Cd and Ni and about 3.4% of K. The fraction 1–3 mm contains 48% and 19% of Ni and Cd, respectively. Furthermore, not negligible concentrations of Sn and Co (4.8% both), as well as of K and Tl (4.1% both), were found. K, present in both fractions, is likely deriving from the electrolyte.

Comparing the chemical composition of the fractions <1 mm and 1–3 mm, a higher concentration of Cd and of Co are observed respectively in the first and in the second one, while Ni resulted constant in both samples. These differences could be due to a different size reduction in the pre-treatment step of the positive electrode (formed by nickel and cobalt hydroxides) and the negative one (constituted by cadmium hydroxide and substrate of nickel), favouring a higher dimensional reduction of the latter. The values resulting in this study are consistent with other literature data ([Nogueira and Margarido, 2004]: Ni: 51%, Cd: 25%, Co: 0.9%;

[TABLE:TABLE_Chemical Characterisation of Spent Rechargeable Batteries_0001]

[TABLE:TABLE_Chemical Characterisation of Spent Rechargeable Batteries_0002]

[Yang, 2003]: Ni: 49–55%, Cd: 41–46%, Co: <3%; [Reddy et al., 2005]: Ni: 61.3%, Cd: 21.4%, Co: 0.5%).

The composition of ferrous fraction, apart from Fe (75%), mainly consists of a not negligible fraction of Ni and Cd; it is likely that these metals, together with K and Co, belong to the residues of dusts of cell material, rather than to the composition of alloy steel. This hypothesis is confirmed by the relative ratios registered in this sample (Ni/Cd: 1.3) and in the powder (Ni/Cd weighted average: 1.2).

According to these results, about 390 g Ni, 330 g Cd, and 20 g Co could be recovered from each kg of powdered material from mixed Ni–Cd spent batteries (respectively, 69%, 83% and 47% of which coming from the finest fraction, <1 mm), besides 110 g of Fe (which was present mainly in the ferrous fraction: 92%).

## 3.2. Ni-MH batteries

## 3.2.1. Weight loss

The weight loss in the case of Ni-MH battery samples was found to be 4.29% for the fine fraction (size <1 mm) and 6.36% for the other one (1 mm < U < 3 mm).

Volatile component can be, as well as in Ni–Cd batteries, ascribed to the water content present in the electrolyte aqueous solution, mainly constituted of diluted potassium hydroxide.

## 3.2.2. Metal content

For the finest fraction, data show a predominance of Ni (that constitutes about 64% in weight), and significant amounts of Co, Tl, Sn, Mn, Fe and K. Also the 1–3 mm fraction appeared mainly enriched in these same metals, as well as in Zn.

These data reflect clearly the composition of the electrodes of this type of battery. The cathode, the same used for the Ni–Cd batteries, is constituted of nickel and cobalt hydroxide. Comparing the concentration of these two metals in the fraction 1 mm < U < 3 mm of the first two kinds of batteries examined, it is possible to note a consistency: Ni / CoNi-Cd = 10 and Ni / CoNi-MH = 10.3. This means that for both kinds of batteries, in this fraction a higher concentration of cathode elements results.

On the other hand, negative electrode is made up mainly of nickel (high quantities in the fine fraction <1 mm) and rare earth (Pietrelli et al., 2005). This result confirms what was inferred for

Ni–Cd batteries – that the cathode tends to be reduced into finer particles, compared to the anode, during the milling process.

Potassium derives from electrolyte, whereas iron could derive from the metallic alloys, used for the anode.

The values obtained agree well with other literature data (Rabah et al., 2008: Ni: 87%, Cd: 9–10%). Considering these results, it can be observed that about 630 g Ni, 78 g Co and 40 g Fe (respectively, 80%, 84% and 67% of which is in the finest fraction) could be recovered from 1 kg of mixed Ni-MH spent batteries. It should be noted that this study did not analyse a number of rare earth elements that might have been in these batteries at low concentrations.

## 3.3. Li-ion batteries

## 3.3.1. Weight loss

Weight loss for Li-ion battery samples was 4.67% for the finer fraction and 3.38% for 1 mm < U < 3 mm. These losses can be ascribed to volatile compounds in the electrolyte (as tetrahydrofuran and 1,2-dimethoxyethane) (Contestabile et al., 1999; van Schalkwijk and Scrosati, 2002; Paulino et al., 2008).

## 3.3.2. Metal content

For this type of battery, the two fractions seem to be quite similar: they contain high quantities of Co, Ni and, to a lesser extent, Li.

The 12% copper in the 1–3 mm fraction can be ascribed to wires and connectors.

Assuming the composition of the positive electrode in Li-ion batteries is LiCoO, the concentrations recorded are typical of the active material. In addition, the ratios between molecular weight and concentrations in the two fractions are similar: M WCo / MWLi = 8.5; Co / Li< 1 m _ f r a c t = 8; Co / Li1 - 3 m _ f r a c t = 8.

The values obtained agree well with other literature data (Shin et al., 2005: Co: 22–28%, Li: 2–3%, Ni: about 1%).

Considering these results, it can be observed that about 250 g Co, 110 g Ni, 31 g Li and 120 g Cu (respectively, 86%, 84%, 45% and 86% of which referring to the finest fraction) could be recovered from 1 kg of material from mixed Li-ion spent batteries.

The significant percentage of non metallic (not determined) compounds can be mainly ascribed to the presence of graphite anode and other materials, as carbonates and polymers used in this kind of batteries.

As for the previous types of batteries, also in this case, Pb and Hg concentrations resulted below LQ (limit of quantification), which can be considered evidence of effective separation of other batteries.

## 3.4. Leaching test

Fig. 2 shows pH and conductivity results for the leaching tests. Values of pH found for leachate solutions are always basic and, in the case of Ni–Cd and Ni-MH batteries, highly basic, due to the presence of hydroxides in the electrolytes.

[TABLE:TABLE_Chemical Characterisation of Spent Rechargeable Batteries_0003]

The resulting electrical conductivity (4–11 mS/cm) can be mainly ascribed to the electrolyte dissolution. Indeed, the amount of metals (as reported in Table 3, together with the other ions investigated) is rather limited, and therefore, in all samples, the size reduction and the absence of a barrier as the plastic shell, do not determine a particular increase of heavy metal mobility.

All anions and elements dissolved in the eluates could be related to the electrolyte contents in the battery’s electrodes. In particular, the presence of potassium hydroxide (Ni–Cd and Ni-MH batteries), lithium salts as LiPF LiBF LiAsF (Li-ion batteries) and some sulphate and chloride salts can be inferred. The tests resulted in low leached concentrations of all metals with the exception of lithium and potassium.

The leaching tests did not consider other anions that could be present, including phosphates, arsenates, and borates. In addition, it should be noted that the high pH values found resulted from a specific leaching test and other pH values and other metal concentrations could be found with different leaching conditions. Still, the high pH values suggest great care in handling this material, which would be highly caustic and corrosive coming into contact with water or humidity. Thus, particular attention must be paid in the critical steps of storage and transportation of the material.

## 4. Conclusion

A chemical characterisation of the material obtained from a disassembly process of spent rechargeable batteries was applied to a simple management procedure, suggesting the possibility of recovering significant amount of economical added value materials, in particular metals.

Ni-MH batteries show similar Ni/Co ratio, compared to Ni–Cd ones, in the fraction 1 mm < U < 3 mm, suggesting that for both kinds of batteries in this fraction higher concentrations of cathode elements occurs. Also for Ni-MH samples, significant amounts of metals can be found, for the most part present in the finer powder (U < 1 mm). Finally, metals analysed in the samples from Li-ion batteries resulted in a similar proportion in the two fractions, with a higher concentration (about 85% for Co, Ni and Cu) in the finest one.

Leaching tests resulted in a low metal release in water solution; the registered conductivity and pH values can be ascribed almost only to the dissolution of electrolytes. This leads to the conclusion that a limited metal contamination can occur if the material is put into contact with water and humidity, even if possible handling activities must take into account the high basicity of resulting leachate solutions.

The data obtained from the investigated case study can be usefully employed to estimate the potential flux of elements as Ni, Li, Co and Cd in a suitable separated waste collection, and to set up proper recycling processes, in particular for the recovery of the most valuable metals.

records.content: Leaching tests were performed according to European Standard Procedures (EN – 12457 – 2). All the seven sub-samples were put in contact with distilled water in capped bottles. Liquid to solid ratio was 10/1 and the suspension was agitated by an overhead shaker (5 rpm) for 24 h at room temperature (20 ± 5 °C). Solid residue was separated by filtration. In eluates, pH, F-, Cl-, SO4^2-, NO3- were analysed by ionic chromatography (IC). After acidification (pH = 2 using HNO3) metals were measured using the same methods followed for digested samples.

## 2.4. Leaching test
Leaching tests were performed according to European Standard Procedures (EN – 12457 – 2). All the seven sub-samples (reported in Fig. 1) were put in contact with distilled water in capped bottles. Liquid to solid ratio was 10/1 and the suspension was agitated by an overhead shaker (5 rpm) for 24 h at room temperature (20 ± 5 ^).. Solid residue was separated by filtration. In eluates, pH, F-, Cl-, SO2-, NO- were analysed by ionic chromatography (IC). After acidification (pH = 2 using HNO ) metals were measured using the same methods followed for digested samples.

text_chunk.text:
## 3.2.2. Metal content
For the finest fraction, data show a predominance of Ni (that constitutes about 64% in weight), and significant amounts of Co, Tl, Sn, Mn, Fe and K. Also the 1–3 mm fraction appeared mainly enriched in these same metals, as well as in Zn.
These data reflect clearly the composition of the electrodes of this type of battery. The cathode, the same used for the Ni–Cd batteries, is constituted of nickel and cobalt hydroxide. Comparing the concentration of these two metals in the fraction 1 mm < U < 3 mm of the first two kinds of batteries examined, it is possible to note a consistency: Ni / CoNi-Cd = 10 and Ni / CoNi-MH = 10.3. This means that for both kinds of batteries, in this fraction a higher concentration of cathode elements results.
On the other hand, negative electrode is made up mainly of nickel (high quantities in the fine fraction <1 mm) and rare earth (Pietrelli et al., 2005). This result confirms what was inferred for
Ni–Cd batteries – that the cathode tends to be reduced into finer particles, compared to the anode, during the milling process.
Potassium derives from electrolyte, whereas iron could derive from the metallic alloys, used for the anode.
The values obtained agree well with other literature data (Rabah et al., 2008: Ni: 87%, Cd: 9–10%). Considering these results, it can be observed that about 630 g Ni, 78 g Co and 40 g Fe (respectively, 80%, 84% and 67% of which is in the finest fraction) could be recovered from 1 kg of mixed Ni-MH spent batteries. It should be noted that this study did not analyse a number of rare earth elements that might have been in these batteries at low concentrations.

## 3.3.2. Metal content
For this type of battery, the two fractions seem to be quite similar: they contain high quantities of Co, Ni and, to a lesser extent, Li.
The 12% copper in the 1–3 mm fraction can be ascribed to wires and connectors.
Assuming the composition of the positive electrode in Li-ion batteries is LiCoO, the concentrations recorded are typical of the active material. In addition, the ratios between molecular weight and concentrations in the two fractions are similar: M WCo / MWLi = 8.5; Co / Li< 1 m _ f r a c t = 8; Co / Li1 - 3 m _ f r a c t = 8.
The values obtained agree well with other literature data (Shin et al., 2005: Co: 22–28%, Li: 2–3%, Ni: about 1%).
Considering these results, it can be observed that about 250 g Co, 110 g Ni, 31 g Li and 120 g Cu (respectively, 86%, 84%, 45% and 86% of which referring to the finest fraction) could be recovered from 1 kg of material from mixed Li-ion spent batteries.
The significant percentage of non metallic (not determined) compounds can be mainly ascribed to the presence of graphite anode and other materials, as carbonates and polymers used in this kind of batteries.
As for the previous types of batteries, also in this case, Pb and Hg concentrations resulted below LQ (limit of quantification), which can be considered evidence of effective separation of other batteries.

text_chunk.text:
## 3.4. Leaching test
Fig. 2 shows pH and conductivity results for the leaching tests. Values of pH found for leachate solutions are always basic and, in the case of Ni–Cd and Ni-MH batteries, highly basic, due to the presence of hydroxides in the electrolytes.
The resulting electrical conductivity (4–11 mS/cm) can be mainly ascribed to the electrolyte dissolution. Indeed, the amount of metals (as reported in Table 3, together with the other ions investigated) is rather limited, and therefore, in all samples, the size reduction and the absence of a barrier as the plastic shell, do not determine a particular increase of heavy metal mobility.
All anions and elements dissolved in the eluates could be related to the electrolyte contents in the battery’s electrodes. In particular, the presence of potassium hydroxide (Ni–Cd and Ni-MH batteries), lithium salts as LiPF LiBF LiAsF (Li-ion batteries) and some sulphate and chloride salts can be inferred. The tests resulted in low leached concentrations of all metals with the exception of lithium and potassium.
The leaching tests did not consider other anions that could be present, including phosphates, arsenates, and borates. In addition, it should be noted that the high pH values found resulted from a specific leaching test and other pH values and other metal concentrations could be found with different leaching conditions. Still, the high pH values suggest great care in handling this material, which would be highly caustic and corrosive coming into contact with water or humidity. Thus, particular attention must be paid in the critical steps of storage and transportation of the material.

final.name: EN 12457-2 leaching test
final.content: Leaching tests were performed according to European Standard Procedures (EN – 12457 – 2). All the seven sub-samples were put in contact with distilled water in capped bottles. Liquid to solid ratio was 10/1 and the suspension was agitated by an overhead shaker (5 rpm) for 24 h at room temperature (20 ± 5 °C). Solid residue was separated by filtration. In eluates, pH, F-, Cl-, SO4^2-, NO3- were analysed by ionic chromatography (IC). After acidification (pH = 2 using HNO3) metals were measured using the same methods followed for digested samples.
